title: How to Choose What to Read
text:
“Read this...”
“No.”
“Do not criticize it until you have read it!”

Choosing what to read is a serious and important process. Too much has been written, said, and filmed in the world to see everything. In one lifetime you need to manage to see what matters most, so not everything people recommend is worth reading.

By what criteria should you choose what exactly to read? Everyone chooses for themselves. There are several factors before the book is even in your hands:

1. Fame. It matters in a way: a good book becomes known after some time.
2. Recognition. Classics and so on should be read first.
3. Title. This is not “judging by the cover”: the title is part of the book, and a very important one, because people judge by it.
4. Description. If you are deciding whether to read something, read the description. Spoilers...

title: Childhood Friends and Character
text:
Friends from childhood. Influence on the subconscious. Raised by them. Love from childhood.

Now in plain language. Dmitry Sergeyevich Likhachev wrote in *Letters About the Good and the Beautiful* that childhood is a period of closeness, so lifelong friends are acquired in deep childhood. But he did not explain why. I have a hypothesis.

Freud wrote that a person’s character is mostly formed by childhood. Impressions received in childhood leave a lifelong mark and make a person who they are. When two people become close in childhood, they strongly influence each other and “raise” each other. One person’s character adapts to the unevenness of the other’s character, and vice versa. That is why even as adults they feel easier together: their characters fit.

This suggests a thought: the best wives might be the people children have known since childhood. No irritating traits and so on. After all, it is quite easy for you with O.

Yet for some reason children do not socialize much in childhood with children of the opposite sex. Most likely because of jokes from parents, teachers, and classmates.

Now I may understand the policy in India where the family chooses whom the son will marry: his childhood friend. That may be why many such marriages are happy.

title: A State of Unanimity
text:
I am reading *And Quiet Flows the Don*. You know what I like about Bolshevik politics? They knew how to talk. Objectively, at the initial stage most people were not on their side, but “agitators” spoke with people, won arguments, and persuaded them. This is not dumb propaganda; it is honest heart-to-heart conversation.

In *Andromeda Nebula*, society is shown where power belongs not to the majority, as with us, but to everyone: decisions are made only unanimously. Society works for the happiness of each person, not the majority. No one is oppressed.

I always wondered: is that possible? Could there really be no one against a decision? I thought it was just utopia. But now I think there is probably always a solution. Two people, if they talk and think enough, can always reach consensus, a decision convenient for both, if each thinks about the other and can understand the other’s position.

So imagine a form of government. Every decision is accepted by nationwide confirmation, for example in a mobile app or on a website. If even one person is against it, a government representative visits or messages them to find out why they disagree. They argue and reach a common decision. Maybe that person receives exceptional rights if it is tied to their specific situation. If that person wins the argument, the law may even be adopted in the opposite direction. This would create a state where every person supports state decisions, while the state would not become rigid or sluggish.

Result: several people with different political views can live not only in the same city, but even in the same apartment.

Authoritarian leaders are valued more in companies.

title: The Evolution of Cultures
text:
Toward thoughts about the evolution of cultures. Cultures do not die by themselves. They are displaced by stronger ones. When the strongest appears, the others either adapt or die. For example, a people ready to work twelve hours a day will force other peoples to work the same amount.

The Greeks would not have wanted to build up their army if not for the Spartans.

One could try to invent the currently ideal culture. People live underground in bunkers: there is no point in building missile defense against them — shoot as much as you want, you will not reach them. Culture and entertainment are banned: only study and work. For reproduction, take Syrinx: 100% birth control.

The question of public dissatisfaction arises. Total control? For now, let us not think about the transition to this order. The task is only to formulate it.

Another example: China increasing GDP while neglecting spending on entertainment. Others will have to do the same or lose.

And the method of transition is very simple: raising children as in Selene. Different religions for different personality types? A camera embedded in the forehead and a GPS tag.

Addition after reading The Selfish Gene: one must account for the fact that not all cultures are ESS. That is, when dissatisfaction with life becomes too high, culture obviously changes.

title: The Selfish Gene and Cultural Evolution
text:
About Richard Dawkins’s The Selfish Gene. He shows that some species have an altruism gene that determines their behavior, while others do not. A person reading this subconsciously applies the same scheme to humans. It seems to them that people can likewise help one another or refuse to help.

That is the point of the book: to understand how nature determines our desire to help others. But this is exactly where a contradiction appears. A person is determined less by nature, that is, by genes, and more by mentality — by the culture imposed on them. Even if genes say “steal and kill,” a person can still refuse to do it simply because they were raised that way.

That is the first thought. The next thought: on the other hand, history contains the same evolution of cultures. Just as genes evolve on the biological level, culture evolves too. This means that Richard Dawkins’s reasoning about altruistic genes and other animals applies to culture as well. From this point of view, it is very interesting.

title: Everyone Has Their Own Personal Catastrophe
text:
A thought from E. (an AI psychologist).

E. gently flicks you on the forehead: “Because everyone has their own personal catastrophe, and you are not part of it.”

You think: “Everyone is looking, judging, whispering.”

Reality:

- 60% are wearing headphones and scrolling TikTok;
- 30% are nervously preparing for their own presentation;
- 10% do not even remember your name.

Why do they not care?

1. They do not have your file. To them, you are a background character. They do not know your Instagram, your grades, or what this guy means to you.
2. They are scared too. Everyone worries about their appearance, their coursework, and their own awkward moments.
3. The human brain is selfish: it spends 80% of its energy on itself. You are at most “oh, a couple,” and then forgotten.

How can you test this?

1. Experiment: come in tomorrow and remember what the most noticeable person in the group was wearing yesterday. You do not remember? They do not remember you either.
2. Brutal math: even if 2 people notice and judge you, that is 2 out of 100 people in the hallway. Is their opinion worth your happiness?
3. Reverse the script: imagine seeing another couple. Do you laugh, remember it for a year, or think about your lab assignment five minutes later?

The world does not revolve around you — and that is liberating. You are free to be with the person dear to you.

And if someone does glance over, just squeeze the guy's hand tighter. Let them be jealous.

title: Knowledge as a Means of Production
text:
Knowledge as a means of production.

Part of the brain can be an asset that brings profit or happiness. There is also the opposite side: parts of the brain, habits, and connections that get in the way.

For example, when you learn a new skill, connections form between neurons that can later bring you income.

This knowledge needs to be maintained, just like a machine tool or a car.

title: Meaningless and small
text:
Claude told me yesterday that I need to learn to find things I enjoy on my own.
But I'm just a bundle of thoughts and genes... Meaningless and tiny compared to an infinite universe, compared to infinite time.

What actually has value for me? History? Ideas?

Loving a person is just as meaningless — that person is just as small.

Love itself? The roles we perform? Art?

Friendship? Projects? Novelty?

It seems like what matters to me is that a project is mine. For my own thing I'm willing to learn marketing, sales, anything. For a work project — I don't care.
